description:
We are a team of motivated university students dedicated to the development of a solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenges 2026. We come from differing majors, including CS, software & mechanical engineering, and finance.

Skills: Front & Backend Development, Physics Simulations, Statistical Modelling, and Analysis via Numerical Methods
summary:
AirSweep is a global health tracker that takes real-world satellite data from NASA's EIC Database and transforms it into an audio experience for the user. By mapping the data onto a globe, a rotating sweep is done across the world from the North to South poles. Depending on the data requested, highs and lows of the measured metric are turned into sounds for the listener, effectively turning coordinates into a soundscape. By mapping air hazards such as Carbon Monoxide and Nitrogen Dioxides onto the globe, users can then hear where the most significantly impacted areas are.

AirSweep is designed for the visually-impaired, but also gives an intuitive understanding of which areas on the planet have higher risks of living. The seamless transitions between the measured metrics also allows health organizations to gather all the needed information at ease, instead of combing through a plethora of different reports and documents.

Air pollution and quality is linked to millions of deaths every year, and having an efficient program to comb through all the data, and make it easy-to-understand for listeners of all levels is crucial.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Air Sweep turns NASA's pictures of air pollution into sound. A realistic 3D Earth rotates beneath a fixed line running from pole to pole. The line works like a record needle: whatever air lies under it is what you hear. North sounds high and south sounds low, and the app plays the strongest hotspots on the line as separate notes.

There are two views. "Air quality and health" uses NASA GMAO maps of near-surface PM2.5, ozone, nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide. "Particles in the air" uses NASA's aerosol visualization, separated by colour into soot, dust, sulfate and sea salt.

For air quality, every pixel is matched to NASA's published colour bar to recover real units, then compared with WHO health guidelines. Each pollutant has its own instrument, shaped by its health effect. PM2.5 is breathing and a heartbeat that quicken; ozone is a whistle that trembles; nitrogen oxides are an engine that revs; carbon monoxide is a slow drone. A signal sounds when the line crosses a guideline. A health report ranks countries and replays each hotspot.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Earth science data is almost entirely visual. Air Sweep lets blind and low-vision people explore global air pollution by ear, with full keyboard and screen-reader support and a plain-language reading under the globe. For everyone else, sound adds an emotional layer that a colour map lacks. The aim is to make the health cost of air pollution, linked by WHO to 4.2 million early deaths in 2019, easier to understand.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with no frameworks

- WebGL with a custom shader for the globe

- Web Audio API for all sound, synthesized live in the browser

- Python with NumPy, SciPy and Pillow to process the NASA frames

- Data: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (items 5669 and 5151 to 5154), Natural Earth for borders and names, Solar System Scope for the Earth surface texture (CC BY 4.0)

- Health references: WHO air quality guidelines, US EPA air quality index guidance

- AI: the project was built with Claude, an AI model by Anthropic, directed by the project author. AI generated the application code, the sound design, the data-processing scripts and the text in the app. The data, maps and Earth imagery are not AI-generated. This is also stated in the app and in the repository README.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The jukebox idea is taken literally: the planet is the record and a line of light is the needle. The instruments are health metaphors, so the sound tells you what a pollutant does to the body, and gets more urgent as levels pass the health guideline.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: values come from NASA's own colour bars, and the app states that they are single-moment model values, not measurements or medical advice.

- Musicality: notes are held to a scale and limited to a few voices so the result is music, not noise.

- Honesty: comparisons with WHO guidelines are labelled as rough, and limits are listed in the app.

- Accessibility and plain language, following health-content guidance.
